section_summary: Pages 94–145 conclude a series of appendices on Japan’s wartime control societies, industrial reorganization, export controls, and national policy companies. Pages 146–168 begin a September 1945 Foreign Economic Administration report on the Japanese fishing industry, including its contents and tables, a prewar survey, wartime shortages and rationing, and the opening discussion of government administration.

people.name: Kichihiko Taniguchi
people.role: Professor; author of “The Link System in Japan”

subfiles.title: Appendix X: Electrical Engineering Control Society in Japan (abstract)
subfiles.about: Describes the establishment, duties, leadership, and departments of an electrical engineering control society.
subfiles.summary: The Tokyo-based society oversees electrical machinery production, allocation, prices, supplies, and research under government direction. The abstract cites the February 1943 Toseikai Nenkan.

subfiles.title: Appendix XI: Electric Machine Control Society (abstract)
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Electric Machine Control Society’s rules for membership, business control, officers, meetings, finance, and dissolution.
subfiles.summary: The society coordinates the manufacture and distribution of electric machines, resources, prices, standards, and research. Its president is appointed by the Minister of Commerce and Industry. The rules also cover governance, member levies, dissolution, and fines.

subfiles.title: Appendix XII: Regulations Governing the Establishment of a Warehouse Control Society
subfiles.about: Outlines a warehouse control society intended to coordinate storage and transport at six major harbors.
subfiles.summary: The proposed society would manage harbor warehouses, coordinate with local control unions and transport businesses, direct essential goods, and protect stocks from air raids. Operations were to begin on 1 May 1944.

subfiles.title: Appendix XIII: Control of Electrical Engineering Industries
subfiles.about: Reports plans to reorganize electrical engineering firms into regional companies and control associations.
subfiles.summary: The Ministry of Munitions sought to organize roughly 5,000 firms to improve resource use, cooperation with power distributors, and air raid readiness.

subfiles.title: Appendix XIV: Regulations on Lumber and Charcoal Production
subfiles.about: Summarizes local governors’ powers over tree cutting, lumber sales, and charcoal production and shipping.
subfiles.summary: Governors designate cutting and sales terms for lumber and production and shipment terms for charcoal.

subfiles.title: Appendix XV: Pit Wood Control Association
subfiles.about: Describes a Northern Kyushu association controlling pit wood supplies for coal mines.
subfiles.summary: The association coordinates mine timber, lowers producers’ costs, and supports transport through a 7.5 million yen fund.

subfiles.title: Appendix XVI: Regulations of the Woolen Goods Control Society
subfiles.about: Sets out the Woolen Goods Control Society’s membership, powers, officers, conferences, accounts, and penalties.
subfiles.summary: The society controls woolen goods production, distribution, supplies, prices, and research. Its regulations establish a Tokyo headquarters, government approved leadership, member conferences and fees, and penalties for violations.

subfiles.title: Appendix XVII: Control Regulations of the Japan Bicycle Control Society
subfiles.about: Summarizes permission, materials, inspection, distribution, and penalty rules for bicycle manufacture and repair.
subfiles.summary: Manufacturers require society approval to make or remake bicycles and must follow its directions on materials, production, inspections, and deliveries. Affiliated associations distribute bicycles and repair goods under prescribed quotas.

subfiles.title: Appendix XVIII: Essential Materials Supervision Corporation Law
subfiles.about: Explains the government funded corporation’s authority to stockpile, purchase, sell, and arrange storage of essential materials.
subfiles.summary: Law No. 69 created a 20 million yen corporation for wartime reserves and efficient use of vital materials. The law took effect on 5 March 1942.

subfiles.title: Appendix XIX: Regulations of Small Scale Business Control Society
subfiles.about: Describes the control of small businesses in Tokyo and Osaka through a financial control society.
subfiles.summary: The rules cover compulsory oversight of member firms, capital and loans, officers, conferences, fees, dissolution, and fines.

subfiles.title: Appendix XX: Middle and Small Scale Industries
subfiles.about: Reviews the wartime consolidation of medium and small industries and the growing powers of control societies.
subfiles.summary: The abstract gives 1942 counts and capital figures for industrial associations and limited companies. It contrasts earlier voluntary associations with compulsory control societies and describes government powers over production, organization, transfers, and closures.

subfiles.title: Appendix XXI: Export Associations
subfiles.about: Explains the growth and wartime purposes of exporters’ associations.
subfiles.summary: Associations sought foreign exchange and war materials while curbing domestic use of exportable goods.

subfiles.title: Appendix XXII: Regulations Governing Special Responsibilities in Keeping Miscellaneous Articles for Export
subfiles.about: Describes designated companies and factories authorized to purchase and safeguard goods for future export.
subfiles.summary: Five companies were assigned to preserve selected export goods and coordinate designated factories, raw materials, and shipments under ministry supervision. The commentary links the scheme to postwar trade plans and foreign exchange needs.

subfiles.title: Appendix XXIII: The Commodity Link System in Japan
subfiles.about: Explains how export obligations and import privileges were linked for selected commodities.
subfiles.summary: Introduced in 1937, the system tied permitted imports to exports through individual or group arrangements. The note lists seven commodity links and describes the cotton trade as a leading example.

subfiles.title: Appendix XXIV: Development of the Commodity Link System in Japan
subfiles.about: Tabulates commodity links, enforcement dates, linked imports and exports, system types, and participating associations.
subfiles.summary: The table covers soap, brushes, wool, hats, Japanese paper, cotton, and rayon.

subfiles.title: Appendix XXV: The National Policy Companies of Japan — 1943
subfiles.about: Lists national policy companies with establishment dates, authorized capital, and paid up capital.
subfiles.summary: The register spans banking, agriculture, fisheries, food, metals, chemicals, textiles, trade, fuels, utilities, transport, medicine, and housing. It includes marine products, fishing net, canned crab, and other fishery related companies. A 1943 company directory is cited as its source.

subfiles.title: Japanese Fishing Industry
subfiles.about: Surveys Japanese fisheries and introduces recommendations for their administration during the occupation.
subfiles.summary: The cover warns that the report’s recommendations were largely written before Japan’s surrender. Its foreword, contents, lists of tables and figures, and opening chapters outline prewar fishing’s importance to food supply and trade. The text describes wartime losses of boats, crews, fuel, equipment, and catch, followed by fish rationing, uneven distribution, black markets, and price controls. Page 168 begins the account of prewar government regulation and licensing.
